newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Lufthansa walkout to cost 20 mln dmk.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Lufthansa walkout to cost 20 mln dmk.

text.p: Germany's Lufthansa AG said a two-hour work stoppage on Thursday, the second in five weeks, by flight-crew and aircraft technicians angry with a long-running pay dispute, would cost it about 20 million marks ($12.94 million).
The airline said it was forced to cancel some 92 European flights for the day, affecting about 6,500 passengers. The walkout took place from 0530 GMT to 0730 GMT at five German airports.

About 1,500 Lufthansa workers left their jobs at the country's largest airports, including its main hub in Frankfurt as well as Munich, Berlin, Hamburg and Duesseldorf, the DAG white-collar workers' union said in a statement.
The union warned that Lufthansa would face further labour troubles and possibly all-out strike action if it refused to change its position in the bitter wage dispute.

Lufthansa said it used Boeing 747 and Airbus A-340 aircraft, typically used for intercontinental routes, for special flights to London, Hamburg and Munich during the peak morning travel hours. They were staffed with management crews.

"We used extra-large planes on the most important routes to take account of the situation and we hope to have things back to normal very soon. But delays cannot be ruled out," Lufthansa spokesman Christian Klick said.

The walkout was called after talks between Lufthansa and the DAG were broken off on Monday night over the length of a new contract as well as over holiday time and Christmas bonuses. The last one-year contract expired on September 30.
Union negotiators are trying to improve a contract approved in October by the OeTV public sector workers' union, which represents ground personnel at Lufthansa.
The two-year OeTV contract calls for workers to receive a one-off payment equal to one-third of a month's base pay and a 1.7 percent pay raise in 1998.
It also includes a payment of either 500 marks in cash or 625 marks in Lufthansa stock as part of a unique profit-sharing scheme for a company still paritally state-owned.

The airline has said it would not negotiate a different contract with the DAG and found the walkouts "incomprehensible". The first DAG work stoppage on November 11 cost Lufthansa about 12 million marks and forced it to cancel about 35 flights.
The DAG union has demanded that the Frankfurt-based airline offer a contract with a shorter duration than the current offer of 27 months and a higher wage offer.

Airline workers are in particular concerned the contract would cover April 1997 when European airline laws are liberalised and full competition threatens Lufthansa's ability to compete because of the relatively high wages in Germany.

A Lufthansa official said pilots at Lufthansa can earn base salaries ranging from 65,000 marks to 247,000 marks, while flight attendants earn from 31,000 to 83,000 marks -- among the highest in the worldwide airline industry.
Workers are also concerned that Lufthansa will seek to move jobs abroad and form new regional airline partnerships with lower operating and wage costs that could threaten jobs.

The airline has been seeking concessions to help cut costs after it reported a 14 percent drop in pre-tax profit for the first nine months in 1996 to 434 million marks despite predictions for a recovery in profits in 1997.
